question: What does a small figure reveal that a monument cannot?
summary: Olmec-associated communities reshaped ground, made containers and figures, and worked stone in different Gulf Coast settings. A small ceramic body, buried floors and workshop traces expose different kinds of activity. Comparing them connects spectacular objects to practical work while preserving each source’s scale and uncertainty.

sections.title: Build a place to live
sections.text: At San Lorenzo, people enlarged raised ground with earth filling and terraces. Making a settlement required repeated work moving and spreading material, alongside building homes and places to gather. The construction history reaches earlier than this dossier’s c. 1200–400 BCE artistic frame. A settlement’s phases and an object-based teaching window answer different questions; neither defines every community called Olmec.

sections.title: Work leaves different traces
sections.text: Earth buildings are less immediately conspicuous than colossal stone heads. Prepared floors nevertheless reveal investment in living spaces and different construction materials. Researcher Ann Marie Cyphers reports unfinished sculptures, tools and abrasive remains near the building called the Red Palace. These connect spectacular stone objects to skilled production. Her reconstruction combines residential, production, storage and ritual spaces; those are interpretations rather than a surviving list of workers and offices. Potters also varied clay, shape and surface treatment to make bowls, rounded containers and figures.

sections.title: Food belonged to particular places
sections.text: Supplying a settlement also meant using its surroundings. Researchers investigate food through plant and animal remains and vessel residues, which preserve differently. A separate study compared the San Carlos homestead with La Joya and Tres Zapotes and found differing maize and fruit frequencies. Its abstract relates variation to wetland access and developing political settings. Such differences make it harder to picture all Olmec households using the same crop in the same way. They do not supply a measured menu for this figure’s maker.

sections.title: A small body changes the question
sections.text: The 17-centimetre ceramic figure focuses attention on bodily display: modeled hands, feet, coiffure and prominent ear ornaments. The museum links adornment to possible social identification and discusses interpretations of intimate ritual handling. A small figure could be held and repositioned, unlike a large fixed monument. Its catalogue supplies no excavated findspot, so it cannot furnish a San Lorenzo household biography.

sections.title: Several centres had different histories
sections.text: San Lorenzo was not the whole story. INAH distinguishes its conventional 1200–900 BCE peak from La Venta’s 800–400 BCE peak. La Venta’s platforms and buried greenstone offerings show a different monumental setting. Shared materials and styles invite regional comparison while leaving room for distinct communities, histories and practices.

deeperReading.title: Why a house count changes
deeperReading.text: A visible mound can look like a convenient household counter. At San Lorenzo an early estimate used low mounds as supposed Olmec dwellings; later work assigned those mounds to the much later Late or Terminal Classic period and rejected the estimate. The correction changed which population the evidence could describe. Merely counting more carefully would not have solved the dating error.

citations.locator: Printed p. 134 / PDF 18: rejected surface-mound estimate

deeperReading.title: From a sample to an estimate
deeperReading.text: Researchers turned to buried surfaces. Excavations helped identify prepared floors; auger samples recorded soil, depth and position. Analysts then grouped evidence by construction phase and location to identify concentrations consistent with buildings. This is a chain of interpretation, not a photograph of every occupied house. A floor may survive without its entire room, and a group of sampled floors still needs a defensible explanation. Estimating inhabitants adds another step: the 2020 study discusses an analogy with households in the local modern community of Tenochtitlán and explicitly acknowledges that ancient and present domestic groups are different. An estimate therefore joins archaeological observations to assumptions about how people shared space.

deeperReading.title: Read the body with the same care
deeperReading.text: The figure raises a parallel problem. Ear ornaments are visible; their wearer’s precise office is not. The museum proposes meanings through comparison with other figurines and burials, including evidence from Tlatilco. Those comparisons supply possibilities rather than this object’s missing findspot. Asking what an observation can support lets small objects and large settlements illuminate ordinary lives without turning either into a complete picture of one uniform society.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded Gulf Coast account, deeper source interpretation, photograph-based family task and source-qualified reference phases. Existing ceramic figure and the complete original case interval retained. No new media or place study added in this module.
limitations: San Lorenzo’s 2020 construction scheme, INAH museum peak conventions, the original case interval and the figure’s catalogue date answer different questions and remain separate.
Only selected 2020 article pages and public 2018 excerpts were consulted. Paid complete articles, the 2014 digital atlas, the 2020 population book and full excavation reports were not read.
The 2012 foodways paper was consulted only in publisher abstract and metadata. No unconsulted sample sizes, precise diet percentages or universal subsistence package adopted.

The UNAM account reports a researcher’s lecture. Finds, proposed room functions and conclusions about political control are not interchangeable. Exact labour, population, status and collapse claims remain outside this expansion.
The catalogue supplies no excavated findspot for the selected figure. Social identification, life-stage and ritual proposals are attributed interpretations, not recovered household biographies.
No universal mother-culture origin, one Gulf Coast polity, precise political succession, language, ethnicity or new relationship with Lapita or Poverty Point inferred.
